Article Title: Martin Phipps and Paramour agree to vacate San Antonio’s River Walk building after a $1.2 million fraud verdict and years of legal battles
Article Text:
Representative Image of a courtroom scene depicting a legal dispute over a San Antonio property sale between longtime friends (AI-generated image)

How the $11 million San Antonio property sale became a legal dispute

Paramour eviction dispute: unpaid rent claims and repeated lockouts

The $1.2 million jury verdict and the ruling on ownership

Martin Phipps and Paramour agree to surrender their spaces

A property sale between longtime friends in San Antonio has developed into a protracted legal dispute, with attorney Martin Phipps and his rooftop cocktail bar, Paramour, agreeing to surrender their spaces in a River Walk building. In late 2022, Phipps’ company, Emet LLC, agreed to sell the property at 102 Ninth St. to CDC Enterprises LP for $11 million. The deal later unravelled over a disputed $2.75 million arrangement involving the purchase price and prepaid rent, alongside allegations of unpaid rent. In late October 2025, a jury found that Phipps and his companies had committed fraud against CDC and awarded the company more than $1.2 million in damages and attorneys’ fees. The dispute continued through eviction proceedings and repeated lockouts. On October 9, 2026, the parties signed agreements requiring Phipps’ law firm and Paramour to surrender their spaces, with a limited period to remove their belongings. The agreements resolve the immediate eviction proceedings but do not establish that every financial or contractual dispute arising from the sale has been settled.In late 2022, Phipps’ company, Emet LLC, agreed to sell the building at 102 Ninth St.to CDC Enterprises, a company associated with Daren Connel, a longtime friend of Phipps. The purchase price was $11 million. According to the San Antonio Express-News, CDC financed $8.25 million of the $11 million transaction, while the remaining $2.75 million was treated as a debt in place of a cash down payment. Phipps maintained that the amount was to be credited as prepaid rent for his law firm and Paramour. CDC disputed that interpretation.Phipps maintained that the parties had agreed to treat the $2.75 million as prepaid rent credit for his law firm and Paramour. CDC disputed that interpretation, and the disagreement became central to the litigation. The building, constructed by Phipps in 2014, houses his law firm and Paramour, a rooftop cocktail bar operated by Holy Spirits LLC. The building, commonly known as the Phipps Building, has since been referred to as Paradigm, the name shown on a leasing sign described in later reporting. CDC’s ownership was upheld in the trial court, while Emet retained a contractual right to buy back the building until late 2027, subject to the terms of the agreement. The dispute illustrates how a property sale can become complicated when financing arrangements, rent credits and commercial leases are linked. The parties’ disagreement over the $2.75 million arrangement became part of a wider conflict involving ownership, unpaid rent and possession of the premises.The disagreement extended beyond the sale contract into disputes over rent and possession of the building. In January 2024, CDC sued Holy Spirits LLC, which operates Paramour, seeking about $260,000 in alleged unpaid rent, fees and interest. CDC claimed the bar had failed to pay rent for several months. Phipps disputed the landlord’s position and argued that CDC owed money in connection with the property. These were competing claims made during the dispute, rather than findings that either party had established every allegation. In February 2024, a justice of the peace ruled in CDC’s favour in an eviction case against Holy Spirits. The company appealed the ruling later that month, moving the dispute into county court, according to the San Antonio Express-News.The conflict also led to repeated lockouts. In 2024, Phipps accused CDC of unlawfully locking out his law firm and Paramour. The dispute resurfaced in March 2026, when CDC again locked out the tenants, citing alleged unpaid rent and common-area maintenance charges. On March 18, 2026, a judge ruled that the March 2 lockout was unlawful because CDC had changed the locks without providing the required 14-day notice. The ruling did not prevent CDC from pursuing eviction through the legal process. In September 2026, CDC locked out Paramour and Phipps’ law firm for the third time since June 2024, according to the San Antonio Express-News. The landlord cited alleged unpaid rent. The lockout led to further eviction proceedings, with cases scheduled for trial on October 9. The parties signed agreements that day requiring the tenants to surrender their spaces, according to the San Antonio Express-News.A major turning point came in late October 2025, when a jury ruled against Phipps and his companies in the dispute over the building. According to the San Antonio Express-News, the jury found against Phipps and his companies on CDC’s fraud claims and awarded CDC more than $1.2 million in damages and attorneys’ fees. The jury awarded Phipps’ companies nothing on their own claims. Phipps, Emet LLC, Holy Spirits LLC, his law firm and his property management firm had countersued CDC on 16 claims, including a claim seeking to have the sale contract declared void and unenforceable because of alleged fraud. During the trial, Phipps’ lawyer asked jurors to award his clients more than $5 million for lost rental income, prepaid rent and building expenses. The jury did not award them damages.Before the jury returned its verdict, State District Judge Angelica Jimenez ruled in CDC’s favour on the ownership issue, according to the San Antonio Express-News. The ruling established that CDC’s title to the property was superior to any claim by Emet LLC. Bexar County property records identify CDC as the owner. Emet LLC retains a contractual option to buy back the building until late 2027, subject to the agreement’s terms, according to the San Antonio Express-News. The jury verdict did not immediately end the wider dispute. Proceedings over rent and possession continued, with the parties returning to court over the tenants’ right to remain in the building.The latest development came on October 9, 2026, when agreements were signed resolving the pending eviction cases. The agreements require Phipps’ law firm and Paramour to surrender possession of their spaces. The agreements allow them until October 30 to remove their belongings, according to the October 12 San Antonio Express-News report. The agreements were signed on the day the eviction cases were scheduled to go to trial. They resolve those eviction proceedings, but should not be treated as proof that every financial or contractual dispute arising from the building sale has been settled.Paramour has operated at the address since 2015 and is known for its rooftop setting, cocktails and drag brunches. In late July 2026, the bar announced that it was “considering pausing this version of Paramour while we plan the next evolution,” adding that it might be forced to move. The statement did not confirm a relocation or provide a reopening date. The announcement came amid the ongoing dispute with the building’s landlord. In September, CDC locked out Paramour and Phipps’ law firm for the third time since June 2024, according to the San Antonio Express-News.

Article Title: Salma Hayek’s billionaire husband backed Notre-Dame with a €100 million pledge after the 2019 fire; restoration efforts brought the 860 year old historic Paris landmark back in 2024
Article Text:
PC: Forbes

Notre-Dame Cathedral fire in 2019 caused extensive damage to the historic landmark

How Salma Hayek ’s billionaire husband supported Notre-Dame’s restoration

How Notre-Dame was rebuilt after the devastating 2019 fire

Notre-Dame welcomed visitors again in December 2024

A historic landmark restored for future generations

In April 2019, a fire tore through Paris’s Notre-Dame Cathedral, destroying its roof and bringing down its famous spire. The damage threatened parts of a landmark whose history stretches back more than 860 years. Among those who stepped forward to help fund its restoration were French billionaire François-Henri Pinault and his father, François Pinault, who pledged €100 million through their family holding company, according to the New York Post. Actor Salma Hayek ’s husband Pinault, joined other major donors in supporting the rebuilding effort. More than five years later, Notre-Dame reopened in December 2024, welcoming visitors back to its restored interior.According to Friends of Notre-Dame de Paris, the fire broke out on 15 April 2019, sending flames and thick smoke above the Île de la Cité, the historic island in the River Seine where Notre-Dame is located. As emergency crews fought to contain the blaze, part of the cathedral’s roof collapsed and its central spire fell. Images of the burning structure travelled around the world, prompting concern over the survival of one of France’s most recognisable historic buildings.Although the fire destroyed much of the timber roof structure and damaged parts of the cathedral, the main stone structure remained standing. The towers and many of the building’s principal features survived, along with important artworks and religious objects that firefighters and emergency teams helped protect.Notre-Dame had undergone centuries of alterations and repairs, and restoring it would require a careful assessment of the surviving structure before reconstruction could begin. The immediate challenge was to stabilise the building, protect it from further deterioration and determine how its damaged sections could be rebuilt.The pledge placed the Pinault family among the prominent private donors responding to the disaster. François-Henri Pinault, who is married to Hayek, leads Kering, the luxury group associated with luxurious brands. His father founded the business that eventually developed into the group and built a substantial fortune through investments in luxury goods and other sectors.“My father François Pinault and myself have decided to release a sum of €100 million from our Artemis funds, the family holding company, to participate in the effort that will be necessary for the complete reconstruction of Notre-Dame.”The family’s contribution was widely reported in the aftermath of the fire, as wealthy individuals and companies offered financial support for the rebuilding campaign. The donation was intended to help meet the cost of restoring the cathedral, rather than fund a separate project bearing the family’s name.The Arnault family, associated with luxury conglomerate LVMH, and the Bettencourt Meyers family also announced major contributions.The reconstruction was not simply a matter of replacing the sections destroyed by the fire. Specialists had to secure the building, remove damaged materials and develop a plan that respected Notre-Dame’s historic fabric. The work involved traditional craftsmanship alongside modern engineering and conservation techniques.Restoring the roof and rebuilding the spire were among the most visible parts of the project. As reported by Friends of Notre-Dame de Paris, the spire, originally designed by architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc during the 19th century, had become a defining feature of the Paris skyline. Its reconstruction followed the historic design, returning a familiar silhouette to the cathedral.Inside, teams worked on the stonework, vaults, decorative elements and other features affected by the fire, smoke and the subsequent emergency operations. Cleaning and conservation were also necessary to bring the interior back into use.As reported by the BBC, French President Emmanuel Macron had expressed, “We'll rebuild Notre-Dame even more beautifully and I want it to be completed in five years, we can do it.” The cathedral ultimately reopened in December 2024, just over five years and seven months after the fire.Reportedly, the reopening ceremonies took place on 7 and 8 December 2024, bringing together political leaders, religious figures, public officials and invited guests. Hayek and Pinault attended the ceremony on 7 December, when the restored cathedral became the focus of international attention once again.More than 1,500 guests were reported to have attended the event, including world leaders and other prominent figures. The gathering marked a significant moment for Paris, where Notre-Dame has long served as a place of worship and a destination for visitors interested in French history and architecture.The reopening also allowed people to see the results of years of painstaking restoration. The cathedral’s interior had been cleaned and repaired, while the rebuilt roof and spire restored much of its familiar appearance. The work aimed to preserve the character of the historic building while making it possible to continue using it safely.Reportedly, Notre-Dame’s origins date to the 12th century, when construction began under Bishop Maurice de Sully. Building work started around 1163, and the cathedral developed over the following centuries, with major additions and changes shaping the structure seen today. Its long history includes periods of religious and political upheaval, restoration and changing uses.The building is associated with major events in French history and has inspired generations of artists and writers. Victor Hugo’s 1831 novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame helped bring renewed public attention to the cathedral during the 19th century, when its condition had deteriorated and restoration was becoming a pressing concern.
Article Summary: Notre-Dame Cathedral fire in 2019 caused extensive damage to the historic landmark. Among those who stepped forward to help fund its restoration were French billionaire François-Henri Pinault and his father. Actor Salma Hayek ’s husband joined other major donors in supporting the rebuilding effort.

Article Title: A 10-year-old New Jersey girl wrote a poem inspired by her Colombian heritage; her work was picked from thousands of entries to finish in the national contest’s Top 10
Article Text:
Luisa's poem uses the colours of the Colombian flag to reflect her Colombian American identity.

How Luisa found out about her poetry award

How a love for books led Luisa to poetry

Luisa Gonzalez's winning poem (Screengrab: Creative communications' official website)

What is Luisa's winning poem All Stitched Together about?

From local poetry competitions to national recognition

A 10-year-old girl from New Jersey has been named among the Top 10 winners of a national poetry competition in the United States for a poem inspired by her Colombian heritage. Luisa Gonzalez, a fifth-grade student from Cherry Hill, received the recognition for her poem All Stitched Together, which was selected from thousands of entries submitted by students across the country.Luisa secured a place in the grades 4 to 6 category of Creative Communication's Summer 2026 poetry contest. Her poem, listed on the competition's official website, draws on the colours of the Colombian flag to explore her identity as a Colombian American. Through the idea of different colours being joined together, she describes how her two cultural backgrounds form part of who she is.According to South Jersey Media, the idea came to Luisa when she was thinking about the Colombian flag and the way its colours fit together. She wanted her poem to reflect her cultural background while encouraging others to take pride in their own identities.Luisa had participated in the competition several times before and received honourable mentions, but had never reached the Top 10.Reaching the Top 10 was a goal Luisa had been working towards for some time. Her mother, Lauren Gonzalez, knew how much it meant to her because she had continued submitting poems despite not securing a place among the top winners in previous attempts.Lauren shared the competition results with Luisa one morning while she was preparing for school. The news left her excited, particularly because she had finally achieved something she had been trying to accomplish."A smile spread across my face and I jumped up and down!" Luisa told South Jersey Media. "I was so glad I won top 10 because I have never won top 10 before in that contest, so I was thrilled."Luisa's interest in poetry developed from her earlier attempts at storytelling and songwriting. She was already making her own books in first grade, using folded sheets of printer paper for a series she called The Brave Girl Series. In the following years, she began writing songs, and it was a suggestion from her aunt that encouraged her to explore poetry.Reading has also been an important part of her routine. Her mother told South Jersey Media that Luisa frequently reads during everyday activities, including car journeys to soccer practice. Her interest in books and writing eventually led her parents to encourage her participation in poetry competitions and public readings."I first started writing songs before I wrote poems!" Luisa explained. "Once my aunt remarked I would be a great poet after reading my songs, I decided to write poetry as well as songs."With encouragement from her family, Luisa began taking part in local writing competitions and sharing her work at open mic events at Inkwood Books in Haddonfield.Her literary interests extend beyond poetry. She admires the works of Langston Hughes and Maya Angelou, as well as songwriter Dolly Parton and Harry Potter author J K Rowling.Luisa's family continues to maintain a connection with Colombia, where her grandparents live. They travel there every other year and remain in contact through virtual conversations between visits. Her grandparents also visit the family in the United States.Spanish is part of family life, with her father, Francisco, speaking the language to the children at home. Luisa and one of her younger brothers also take Spanish classes locally.These family experiences form part of the cultural background Luisa wanted to express in All Stitched Together. Through the colours of the Colombian flag, she explored what it means to grow up with both Colombian and American identities."Hispanic Heritage means so much to me," she said. "It means to be proud of yourself as a Hispanic, and to be you."Luisa had experience presenting her work to audiences even before receiving the national award. She has taken part in community events, including the Collingswood Hispanic Heritage Festival, and also secured first place in Collingswood's Youth Poetry Contest.However, speaking in front of an audience was initially difficult for her. She said that she worried about making mistakes, especially when presenting one of her poems in Spanish. With experience, she became more comfortable reading her work publicly.Her growing confidence has also been visible at school. According to her mother, Luisa had previously preferred not to tell her school about a local poetry award. This year, she decided to share her achievement with her principal, who responded with encouraging emails and video messages.Luisa, who has three younger brothers, hopes to continue writing as she grows older. She wants to become a teacher, poet and author, and hopes to encourage other children to develop their interests. "I would love to encourage others to stay curious," she said.According to Creative Communication's official website, the other nine students selected as Top 10 winners in the grades 4 to 6 category of the Summer 2026 poetry contest were Patti-Rose Gonzalez, Eugene Wong, Eli Johnson, Hanifa Khan, Henry Wang, Aila Adeline, Anna Zhao, Jayceon Jones and Luke Feirstein.
Article Summary: Luisa Gonzalez's poem All Stitched Together was selected from thousands of entries. The poem uses the colours of the Colombian flag to reflect her Colombian American identity. Luisa had participated in the competition several times before and received honourable mentions, but had never reached the Top 10.

Article Title: In 2012, Barbra Streisand gave $10 million to support a Cedars-Sinai women's heart centre; 14 years later, it provides research-driven cardiac care to more than 1,700 women each year
Article Text:
Photo: Barbra Streisand/ Instagram

Why women’s heart health needed attention

Streisand’s $10 million gift

How women’s heart disease can differ

Research-driven care for women

A legacy of advocacy

Why the centre still matters

In 2012, Barbra Streisand donated $10 million to Cedars-Sinai to create a research centre focused on women’s cardiovascular health. The gift helped establish the Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center, a facility dedicated to understanding why heart disease can affect women differently from men and improving diagnosis and treatment for female patients. According to Cedars-Sinai, the centre now provides research-driven cardiac care to more than 1,700 women each year.The donation was not simply a high-profile act of philanthropy. It responded to a long-standing gap in medicine, where heart disease research has often relied heavily on male subjects while women’s symptoms and underlying conditions can differ. Fourteen years on, the centre remains focused on closing that gap through patient care, research, and education.Heart disease is the leading cause of death among women in the United States. Cedars-Sinai says more than 500,000 women die from cardiovascular disease each year, a figure greater than deaths from all cancers combined.Despite that scale, women have historically been underrepresented in heart-related studies. Streisand’s own website cites a Los Angeles Times report noting that women made up less than a quarter of participants in heart-related studies, while women’s heart disease was also less likely to be properly diagnosed than men’s.Cardiologist Bernadine Healy described the problem as “Yentl syndrome” in 1991, referencing the Streisand film about a woman who had to disguise herself as a man to receive an education. The idea was that women often received proper heart treatment only after showing symptoms that resembled those typically seen in men.Streisand’s $10 million contribution helped fund the Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center at Cedars-Sinai. The donation was part of a broader campaign that raised more than $22 million for research into women’s cardiovascular health.The singer also helped recruit other major donors, including Michael Bloomberg, Barry Diller, Diane von Furstenberg, Ralph Lauren, Irwin Jacobs, Ronald Perelman, Sumner Redstone, and Haim Saban. Several contributed $1 million each, helping expand the centre’s research capacity.Streisand said she had long been angered by inequality, including gender discrimination in medicine. She argued that women deserved the same level of scientific attention and research investment as men, particularly in an area as serious as heart disease.One of the centre’s central goals is to address the fact that heart disease does not always look the same in women and men. Cedars-Sinai explains that men more often experience the classic heart-attack symptom of chest pain during exertion, while women are more likely to report chest pressure, indigestion, shortness of breath, and fatigue.The underlying causes can differ as well. In men, heart disease is most commonly linked to a blocked coronary artery. In women, it is often caused by reduced blood flow in the heart’s small arteries, a condition known as microvascular coronary dysfunction.That difference matters because standard diagnostic tools may not reveal the problem in women. The centre says it is developing new treatment strategies and comprehensive risk assessments based on these biological differences.The Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center provides care to more than 1,700 women annually. Its work combines clinical treatment with research designed to improve how doctors identify and manage cardiovascular disease in female patients.Cedars-Sinai says the centre is one of only a few medical centres worldwide to use an adenosine cardiac magnetic resonance imaging stress test for diagnosing heart disease. The centre says this tool is better than an angiogram, the standard diagnostic approach for men, at revealing microvascular coronary dysfunction in women.The centre’s approach reflects a shift away from treating women’s heart disease as a smaller version of men’s disease. By studying sex-specific symptoms, risk factors, and diagnostic patterns, it aims to help doctors detect problems earlier and tailor treatment more effectively.Streisand’s involvement went beyond writing a cheque. She worked with Dr Noel Bairey Merz, the centre’s medical director, to raise awareness and funding for women’s cardiovascular research. The two also delivered a TED Talk on the issue in the years before the centre’s dedication.Merz said women’s health research was often constrained by political debates and by the perception that heart disease was less urgent than other conditions. She hoped private philanthropy could help stabilise research funding and allow scientists to pursue questions that public grants did not always support.The centre’s work has helped bring greater attention to an issue that affects millions of women. Its focus on research, education, and clinical care reflects Streisand’s belief that women should not have to wait for their symptoms to resemble men’s before receiving appropriate treatment.Fourteen years after the donation, the Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center continues to serve women whose symptoms may be overlooked or misunderstood. Its work remains important because cardiovascular disease continues to kill more women than all cancers combined.The centre also highlights the value of funding research that asks different questions. Instead of assuming that male-focused studies can fully explain women’s heart health, it examines how sex, symptoms, vascular function, and risk factors may interact in distinct ways.Streisand’s gift began as a response to a personal and societal concern, but its impact has endured. By helping create a centre dedicated to women’s hearts, she supported a model of care that treats women’s cardiovascular health as a priority in its own right.
Article Summary: The Barbra Streisand Women’s Heart Center provides care to more than 1,700 women annually. Its work combines clinical treatment with research designed to improve how doctors identify and manage cardiovascular disease in female patients. More than 500,000 women die from cardiovascular disease each year, greater than deaths from all cancers combined.

Article Title: At 11, Aneeshwar Kunchala is set to receive the Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal for his wildlife-conservation work; he began campaigning against plastic pollution at four
Article Text:
An incident that changed his perspective

From wildlife videos to international audiences

Following Jane Goodall's conservation legacy

Jane Goodall spent decades showing the world why protecting animals and their habitats matters to humanity. Now, an 11-year-old conservationist is preparing to carry that message to a younger generation. Aneeshwar Kunchala, a UK-based wildlife presenter with family roots in Andhra Pradesh, India, is set to receive the Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal for his work promoting wildlife conservation and biodiversity. According to The South Asia Times, Kunchala's journey began at just four, when he learnt about a whale that had died after ingesting plastic pollution. The experience inspired him to raise awareness about the threats facing wildlife.The medal was announced by STARMUS, an international festival bringing together science, space exploration, technology, music and the arts. In a statement issued on October 10, the festival named Aneeshwar as the recipient of the Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal, recognising his efforts to encourage children to protect the natural world. The award is scheduled to be presented during STARMUS VIII, taking place in Tenerife and La Palma in Spain's Canary Islands from October 17 to 22, 2026.Kunchala's interest in conservation began in his first year at school. In an interview with National Geographic Kids, he recalled how his teacher showed the class a picture of a whale that had died because of plastic pollution. He was shocked by the image and the fact that discarded plastic could kill such a large animal.The incident stayed with him and prompted him to think about what he could do to help wildlife. Although he was only four, the experience became the starting point for his efforts to educate others about protecting animals and the environment.In 2020, Kunchala began filming videos about animals with his father. Their first video focused on a baby robin in their garden, which he named Regee. The videos gave him an early platform to share his enthusiasm for wildlife and explain why animals and their habitats deserve protection. Over time, his activities expanded into television, documentary presenting, writing, poetry, art and public speaking.One of his major milestones came in 2022, when he presented COP27: Six Ways to Save Our Planet, a documentary addressing ways to tackle environmental challenges. Guinness World Records recognised him as the youngest male documentary presenter for the programme, at seven years and 288 days old.He has since appeared in wildlife and educational programming associated with broadcasters including the BBC, Sky Kids and Channel 5. His work has also included Go Wild with Steve Backshall, a CBeebies programme in which he learnt about animals, conservation and filmmaking alongside the naturalist and television presenter. He has described working with Backshall as one of the most memorable experiences of his career.His achievements extend beyond television. Guinness World Records lists three records associated with his work, including youngest male documentary presenter, youngest male newspaper columnist and the most animal sounds identified in one minute by an individual under 16. In January 2025, he identified 28 different animal sounds in a minute for the latter record. He has also written about endangered animals and used his own drawings and paintings to communicate his interest in nature.In 2024, Kunchala received the Diana Award for his work involving children and wildlife conservation. He has also been recognised through the British Citizen Youth Award and the Young Scientific Explorer honorary award from the Scientific Exploration Society. His other roles include serving as a National Trust ambassador and becoming the first young columnist for National Geographic Kids UK, where he contributes advice on helping wildlife, seasonal nature activities and citizen science projects.The Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal connects Kunchala's work with the legacy of the renowned primatologist and conservationist, who devoted her life to studying chimpanzees and advocating for animal welfare and environmental protection. The medal recognises efforts to preserve biodiversity and encourage greater responsibility towards life on Earth.STARMUS established the Junior recognition to celebrate young people whose work reflects the importance of science, environmental stewardship and public engagement. The festival has also announced the Junior Stephen Hawking Medal for Spanish science communicator Valeria Corrales, highlighting two different ways in which young people can bring scientific and environmental ideas to wider audiences.Kunchaala's approach combines storytelling with practical encouragement, particularly for children who may feel too young to make a difference. In a February 2023 interview with Scouts UK, Kunchala summed up his conservation mission with the words, “Please save the animals and make sure the world looks beautiful.” It reflects the central idea behind his work: that caring about nature can begin with a single experience and grow into sustained efforts to educate others.When asked about his hope for the future, he told National Geographic Kids, "My dream is a future where wildlife is safe, valued and able to thrive alongside humans."
Article Summary: Aneeshwar Kunchala, 11, is set to receive the Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal. He is a UK-based wildlife presenter with family roots in Andhra Pradesh, India. The medal recognises efforts to preserve biodiversity and encourage greater responsibility towards life on Earth.

Article Title: Virginia has acquired 2,211 acres around Buffalo Mountain to create a new conservation area, protecting nearly 14 miles of native trout streams and expanding a landscape already drawing 15,000 visitor
Article Text:
Buffalo Mountain’s new conservation area offers scenic landscapes, protected forests and outdoor experiences near the Blue Ridge Parkway and Blacksburg.

A major expansion of protected land

Protecting forests and trout streams

A destination for outdoor enthusiasts

Conservation with a long-term view

There are landscapes that become part of a place’s identity long before they receive an official designation. Buffalo Mountain, with its rounded summit, expansive views and deep Appalachian forests, has long been one of Southwest Virginia’s most recognisable natural landmarks. Now, more than 2,200 additional acres around the mountain are set to remain protected, giving the landscape a stronger shield against future development, states an online release by the official website of the Commonwealth of Virginia.According to the release, Virginia has established a new State Conservation Area at Buffalo Mountain following the acquisition of 2,211 acres across Floyd and Carroll counties. The property surrounds the existing Buffalo Mountain Natural Area Preserve, creating a larger protected landscape and bringing the total acreage of Department of Conservation and Recreation-owned land at Buffalo Mountain to 4,332 acres, adds the online report.If we go by the release, the acquisition was carried out in partnership with The Conservation Fund, with $9.5 million in federal Forest Legacy Program funding helping make the purchase possible.The newly protected property will be managed by the Department of Conservation and Recreation, which plans to develop a management strategy and expand opportunities for public access.The move builds on decades of conservation efforts in the area. An earlier phase of the project added 975 acres to the existing natural area preserve, taking the dedicated preserve to 2,121 acres, claims the online release.The importance of the acquisition extends well beyond hiking trails and scenic overlooks. The property contains nearly 14 miles of native trout streams, including waterways supporting wild populations of eastern brook trout and brown trout.These streams sit within the headwaters of the New River, an important water source for communities in Virginia and West Virginia. The river provides drinking water to more than 675,000 people, making the protection of surrounding forests and waterways an important part of maintaining water quality.The landscape is also home to extensive mature forests, including Southern Appalachian Rich Cove Forest, a habitat type known for its ecological diversity. Keeping the surrounding acreage intact creates a buffer for the existing natural area preserve while helping protect wildlife habitat and forest connectivity.Located in a rural part of Southwest Virginia, the conservation area lies only a few miles from the Blue Ridge Parkway and less than 50 miles from the growing Blacksburg area. Buffalo Mountain has already established itself as a popular destination, with about 15,000 people visiting the preserve each year, claims the online report.The summit is a major draw, offering broad views across the surrounding Appalachian landscape. With the new conservation area, visitors will eventually have access to more opportunities for low-impact recreation while the most sensitive natural resources remain protected.The project also represents a significant collaboration between state and federal conservation agencies, The Conservation Fund and the Lawson family, which had owned the property for more than a century. The land was acquired by The Conservation Fund before being transferred to Virginia for permanent protection, adds the report.Federal Forest Legacy funding for the purchase comes through the Land and Water Conservation Fund, which supports conservation and recreation projects across the country. With the Buffalo Mountain acquisition, a landscape shaped by generations of private stewardship is now entering a new chapter as public land.Images Courtesy: istock
Article Summary: Virginia has established a new State Conservation Area at Buffalo Mountain following the acquisition of 2,211 acres across Floyd and Carroll counties. The property surrounds the existing Buffalo Mountain Natural Area Preserve, creating a larger protected landscape. The land contains nearly 14 miles of native trout streams, including waterways supporting wild populations of eastern brook trout and brown trout.

Article Title: Explosion, fuel leak: Two Syrian pipelines damaged in fresh blow to war-hit energy network
Article Text:
Security forces of Syria's Interior Ministry guard the al-Omar oil field, the country's largest by area and production

Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday, with one explosion triggering a fire and another causing a fuel leak, Syrian state media reported.According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), citing the state-owned Syrian Petroleum Company, an explosion struck the Jbessa gas pipeline in Hasakah province, while a separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.The explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze.The Syrian Petroleum Company described the incident as sabotage. Officials said alternative arrangements would maintain gas supplies to power stations during repairs, while domestic gas supplies remained unaffected.In a separate incident, a hole was discovered in the Baniyas-Homs pipeline in the Hadida area west of Homs, causing a leak of petroleum products. Emergency and technical teams were deployed to contain the leak and isolate the damaged section.Al Jazeera, citing Syrian state media, reported that the damage to the Baniyas-Homs pipeline was believed to be linked to an attempted fuel theft. The initial reports did not confirm the cause or identify those responsible.The incidents come amid a series of disruptions to Syria’s energy infrastructure. Earlier in October, an oil pipeline near Tal Hamis in Hasakah province was damaged in what the Syrian Petroleum Company described as sabotage.Syria is working to rebuild its oil and gas infrastructure after years of conflict, restoring production in northeastern oilfields and reconnecting them with processing facilities and refineries in Homs and Baniyas.In January 2026, the Syrian Petroleum Company began pumping raw gas from the Jbessa fields in Hasakah to the Furqlus gas plant in Homs countryside at around 1.2 million cubic metres per day to support electricity generation.The second damaged pipeline, connecting Baniyas on the Mediterranean coast to Homs, transports petroleum products between two important energy centres. The Baniyas refinery is undergoing an overhaul aimed at increasing its processing capacity from around 80,000 to 130,000 barrels per day.Syria has also undertaken emergency pipeline repairs and plans to expand its transportation network. A September 2026 analysis by the Baker Institute for Public Policy reported that the Syrian Petroleum Company was repairing existing infrastructure and planning a heavy-crude pipeline linking northeastern oilfields to the Baniyas refinery.
Article Summary: Two pipelines carrying gas and petroleum products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria on Thursday. One explosion struck the Jbessa gas export pipeline in the al-Arabidi area of Hasakah province, setting the pipeline on fire. Emergency teams isolated the damaged section and shut valves to contain the blaze. A separate leak was detected on the Baniyas-Homs petroleum-products pipeline near Homs.

A 19-year-old US man who allegedly told co-workers he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people” was arrested over a suspected mass shooting plot targeting a Hindu temple in Aurora, near Chicago. Police say he had shared a racist manifesto and visited the temple on the day investigators believe he planned to attack.Alexandros Paporakis, a Taco Bell cashier from Palatine, Illinois, faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches. A judge ordered him detained before trial on Wednesday. His next court appearance is scheduled for October 30.According to prosecutors, Paporakis openly identified himself as a white supremacist at work and regularly made disparaging remarks about people of different races, including Indians. His colleagues told investigators that he discussed Nazis and violence and that his behaviour had intensified in the days before his arrest.On Saturday, he allegedly told a co-worker that he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people” and spoke about a plan involving a Hindu temple in Aurora, a city about 65 kilometres southwest of Palatine.He also told a colleague that Sunday would be “a special day”, according to court documents.Prosecutors allege that Paporakis had been planning an attack for about two years, narrowing his focus to a specific location in recent months. He allegedly researched the target using YouTube and Google Street View.Investigators say the material he shared with a co-worker included an eight-page document titled Why I Fought: A.K.A. (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto). According to a court document obtained by the Associated Press, the manifesto described Indian, Jewish and Black people as “subhumans” and outlined a plan to kill as many of them as possible.In the document, Paporakis allegedly described himself as a “sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasising about mass murder nearly every day”. He also portrayed his outward identity as a working college student as a facade concealing his violent intentions, according to the documents.Police believe Paporakis may have attempted to carry out the attack on Sunday, October 11. Surveillance footage showed his car entering the parking lot of a large Hindu temple in Aurora at around 12.25 pm and leaving approximately 13 minutes later. Investigators said he appeared to be alone in the vehicle.The precise intended target has not been officially identified by police and remains under investigation. The Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora subsequently alerted its members to a security threat, according to The New York Times.Prosecutors allege that Paporakis contacted a co-worker later that day and said his gun had jammed. He reportedly said he had left the scene “super fast” without being seen. He also allegedly sent the colleague a video showing the rifle failing to fire and said he wanted to repair it and try again.According to court documents, he told the co-worker that the man he had fired at had been “certainly saved by his God today”. The documents do not establish the identity of the person he allegedly fired at or provide further details about the circumstances.The co-worker contacted police, prompting officers from Palatine and neighbouring Mount Prospect to locate Paporakis. Investigators believed he might attempt to carry out the plan again, and officers arrested him outside his home on Sunday afternoon.A search of Paporakis’ home uncovered an AR-style rifle without a serial number, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of ammunition and tactical equipment, police and prosecutors said. Investigators also recovered a tactical vest with body armour, items bearing Nazi symbolism and a gas canister labelled with an anti-South Asian slur.The evidence, along with the alleged manifesto and electronic communications, is being examined as part of the investigation. The FBI’s Chicago Field Office assisted local police in reviewing the material.“The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated,” Palatine Police Chief William Nord said, describing the protection of places of worship as a law enforcement priority.Ryan Whalen, the FBI’s Chicago special agent in charge, said the agency worked with local and state authorities to identify and investigate threats driven by extremist ideologies. He credited the rapid response by the Palatine and Mount Prospect police departments with ensuring that the suspect was taken into custody without harm to the community.Paporakis has been charged with making a terrorist threat, a Class X felony, and unlawful possession of a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches, a Class 3 felony. It was not immediately clear whether he had entered a plea or secured legal representation.The case has intensified concerns about hostility towards Indian Americans and other South Asian communities in the United States, particularly as anti-immigration rhetoric and disputes over skilled-worker visas have become increasingly contentious.The FBI does not record crimes against Indian Americans as a separate category. Data on anti-Hindu and anti-Sikh offences therefore offer only a partial picture of the hostility faced by communities whose members often trace their roots to India.Physical attacks and vandalism have also affected Hindu places of worship. In June 2025, between 20 and 30 rounds were reportedly fired at a Krishna temple in Spanish Fork, Utah, while people were inside; no injuries were reported. A separate temple in Santa Clara, California, was vandalised later that summer.Online hostility has been more pronounced. A report by the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate found that the monthly volume of hateful posts about South Asians on X more than tripled between January 2024 and June 2026.Researchers have linked some of the hostility to disputes over immigration and the H-1B visa programme, which US employers use to hire skilled foreign workers. Indians receive more than 70% of H-1B visas.The ministry of external affairs also said it was “deeply concerned” by the alleged plot, describing its reported anti-Hindu and racist nature as “particularly disturbing”. Official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal called for a thorough investigation, accountability for those responsible and measures to ensure the safety of the Indian community in the US.
Article Summary: Alexandros Paporakis, 19, faces felony charges of making a terrorist threat and unlawfully possessing a rifle with a barrel shorter than 16 inches. Police say he had shared a racist manifesto and visited the temple on the day investigators believe he planned to attack. He allegedly described himself as a “sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasising about mass murder nearly every day’

Article Title: A 6-year-old Nebraska boy found a rare 200-million-year-old marine fossil that had not been recorded in the state for more than 55 years
Article Text:
PC: Nebraska Game and Parks Commission

How did a 6-year-old boy discover a rare marine fossil

What did experts discover about the rare marine fossil

PC: Nebraska Game and Parks Commission

Why are conulariid fossils dating back 200 million to 500 million years so rare

How will the rare marine fossil help educate visitors

A six-year-old boy searching for fossils at a Nebraska park made a discovery not recorded in the state for more than 55 years. Leo Youngdahl, who lives in Eagle, turned over a large rock at Schramm Park State Recreation Area near Gretna and found the imprint of a conulariid, an ancient marine animal with a jellyfish-like body shaped like an upside-down pyramid. Conulariids lived in Nebraska between approximately 200 million and 500 million years ago. The only other known examples in the state were found in Louisville and Weeping Water. Staff plan to keep the fossil at Schramm for educational programmes.According to People, Leo was at a Rafting and Rocks event at Schramm Park State Recreation Area when he spotted a large rock and decided to turn it over. Outdoor Nebraska states that he hoped to find a crinoid fossil. Crinoids are among his favourite fossils.Leo noticed an unusual pattern on the underside of the rock. It reminded him of the scales on a garter snake's belly. He showed it to Kelly Ekue, an outdoor education specialist at the nearby Schramm Education Centre, who immediately noticed something different about it.Ekue has led programmes at the outcrop for over seven years, and there are six main types of fossils found there.She told Outdoor Nebraska that the fossil looked unlike any of the species she has seen. The imprint was larger than the fossils typically found at the park. It also appeared almost fish-like, even though the rocks there contain fossils of marine invertebrates rather than fish.Ekue was unsure what Leo had uncovered, so she emailed a photograph to a geologist, who shared it with other experts. People named two of them: Shane Tucker, a palaeontologist at the University of Nebraska State Museum, and the geologist Bob Diffendal. The experts identified the fossil as a conulariid, an ancient marine animal with a jellyfish-like body shaped like an upside-down pyramid.Conulariids lived in what is now Nebraska, as well as other parts of the world, between approximately 200 million and 500 million years ago. Their fossils are especially rare because the creatures had soft bodies and thin skeletons that typically broke apart before they could be preserved.Researchers identified Leo's specimen by its distinctive herringbone-shaped pattern, which had left an imprint in the limestone. According to Outdoor Nebraska, the only other known conulariid fossils found in the state were discovered more than 55 years ago in Louisville and Weeping Water.The discovery was exciting for Leo for another reason. He had never found a complete fossil before, especially one so large. He also recalled being told that his find was "rarer to find than a mammoth bone." Ekue said it was amazing that, among all the rocks in the Schramm outcrop, Leo picked up this one, recognised it as a fossil and thought to ask about it. Leo will not be taking the fossil home, and he does not mind. It will remain at Schramm, where staff plan to use it in educational programmes.
Article Summary: Leo Youngdahl turned over a large rock at Schramm Park State Recreation Area near Gretna, Nebraska. He found the imprint of a conulariid, an ancient marine animal with a jellyfish-like body shaped like an upside-down pyramid. Conulariids lived in Nebraska between approximately 200 million and 500 million years ago. The only other known examples in the state were found in Louisville and Weeping Water.

Article Title: Daymond John started FUBU from his mother’s Queens home with a $40 fabric budget and sold $800 of hats in one day; the brand later grew from that tiny start to more than $6 billion in global sales
Article Text:
A small investment that sparked a business

His mother helped keep the dream alive

Hip-hop culture helped FUBU find its audience

From a homegrown label to a global business

Before Daymond John became a familiar face on Shark Tank, he was a young entrepreneur trying to turn a small idea into a clothing business, working from his mother’s home in Queens, New York. According to ABC News and a 2018 account of his career at RECon, the FUBU co-founder began with just $40 for fabric, eventually building a brand that generated more than $6 billion in global sales. His journey highlights how family support, resourcefulness and an understanding of popular culture helped transform a modest venture into a major name in hip-hop fashion.John launched FUBU in 1992, drawing on his interest in fashion and the growing influence of hip-hop culture. With limited money available, he bought approximately $40 worth of fabric and used sewing skills taught to him by his mother, Margot John, to make tie-top hats.He took the finished hats to a street corner in Queens and sold the entire batch in a single day, bringing in $800. The sales offered an early indication that there was a market for clothing that reflected the style and identity of young hip-hop fans.Rather than immediately establishing a conventional manufacturing operation, John and his family began building the business from home.Their living room became a makeshift production space, with his mother playing a central role in helping him pursue the venture.FUBU, short for For Us, By Us, was built around clothing designed for a community that John believed was underserved by mainstream fashion brands. Its identity was closely tied to hip-hop, an emerging cultural force that would go on to influence music, entertainment and global streetwear.Margot John was instrumental in turning the early idea into a business capable of taking larger orders. After the venture struggled to secure conventional financing, she took out a second mortgage on the family home, reportedly releasing around $100,000 in equity to support the company.The financial commitment came after John and his associates faced repeated rejections from banks. ABC News reported in 2016 that 27 lenders had turned them down when they sought funding. His mother also encouraged him to remain persistent while taking responsibility for his ambitions. Her willingness to put the family home at risk demonstrated the confidence she had in his potential, even when outside institutions were reluctant to back the business.John continued working at Red Lobster while developing FUBU, using his earnings to help sustain the venture. The combination of a regular job, family support and an unconventional approach to funding allowed him to continue pursuing growth without the financial backing that many startups seek at the outset.Building the product was only one part of the challenge. John also needed to introduce FUBU to consumers and establish its credibility within the culture that had inspired it. He approached musicians and other emerging cultural figures, encouraging them to wear the brand. One of the most significant connections was with Queens-born rapper LL Cool J , whose association with FUBU helped bring the label to a wider audience.In 1997, LL Cool J wore a FUBU hat in a Gap television commercial and incorporated the brand into a freestyle rap. The appearance became a memorable example of how music, celebrity and fashion could work together to create visibility for a young label. John also pursued opportunities to showcase the clothing at trade events, including a Las Vegas trade show, where he and his team worked to attract buyers and secure orders. As demand grew, the business needed more capital and manufacturing capacity to fulfil its ambitions. A financing opportunity eventually emerged through Samsung Textiles, helping the company move beyond its early limitations. The episode illustrated the importance of persistence and finding unconventional routes when traditional funding options failed.FUBU went on to become one of the defining names associated with the rise of hip-hop-inspired streetwear during the 1990s and early 2000s. Its success demonstrated that a brand rooted in a specific community could reach an international audience by building a clear identity and connecting with its customers. John later expanded his career into entrepreneurship education, writing and television. As an investor on ABC’s Shark Tank, he became known for evaluating businesses and backing entrepreneurs seeking capital and commercial guidance.His experiences also informed his book The Power of Broke, published in 2016, which explores how limited resources can push entrepreneurs to become more inventive and strategic. Rather than treating a lack of money as an automatic barrier, John argues that constraints can encourage founders to make better use of the people, skills and opportunities already available to them.From selling a small batch of hats on a Queens street corner to helping build a multibillion-dollar fashion brand, John’s story reflects the role of cultural insight, persistence and family backing in entrepreneurship. FUBU’s growth was not the result of a single lucky break, but of turning a modest beginning into a business that understood its audience and found ways to reach it.
Article Summary: FUBU, short for For Us, By Us, was built around clothing designed for a community that John believed was underserved by mainstream fashion brands. Its identity was closely tied to hip-hop, an emerging cultural force that would go on to influence music, entertainment and global streetwear. FUBU generated more than $6 billion in global sales.

Article Title: Joni Mitchell moved from Canada to the United States in the mid-1960s and built much of her career there; 62 years later, at age 82, the legendary singer-songwriter has officially become a US citizen
Article Text:
From Canada to the heart of American music

An enduring legacy in music

A new chapter after decades in the US

Canadian-born singer-songwriter Joni Mitchell has officially become a United States citizen, marking a significant milestone in a life and career closely intertwined with American music. As reported by Billboard and the Los Angeles Times, the 82-year-old musician shared news of her naturalisation on October 13, 2026, more than six decades after first arriving in the country. Mitchell announced the development on social media, posting a photograph of herself holding a small American flag alongside footage from her citizenship ceremony. The announcement brings a new chapter to a journey that began in 1965, when she moved to the United States with her then-husband, musician Chuck Mitchell. Although the singer has not publicly explained what prompted her decision to pursue citizenship, the milestone gives her the right to vote in US elections, provided she meets the applicable registration and voting requirements.Born Roberta Joan Anderson on November 7, 1943, in Fort Macleod, Alberta, Mitchell grew up in Saskatchewan before beginning her musical journey across the border. Her early travels took her to Detroit and later New York, before she settled in Southern California.Los Angeles became a defining setting in her artistic life. By the late 1960s, Mitchell was closely associated with Laurel Canyon, the hillside neighbourhood that became a gathering place for influential musicians and songwriters of the era. She shared creative connections with artists including David Crosby and Graham Nash, while developing a distinctive musical identity that blended folk, jazz, pop and deeply personal storytelling. Her move to the United States helped place her at the centre of a changing music scene, but her influence would eventually extend far beyond any one city or genre.Across a career spanning several decades, Mitchell has earned recognition for her songwriting, unconventional musical arrangements and willingness to explore intimate subjects through her work. Her catalogue includes celebrated songs such as Big Yellow Taxi, Both Sides, Now, River and A Case of You. Her 1971 album Blue remains one of her most acclaimed recordings, widely admired for its emotional candour and sparse, expressive arrangements.Another major release, Court and Spark (1974), brought her considerable commercial success, reaching No. 2 on the Billboard 200 chart. Her song Help Me, from the same album, peaked at No. 7 on the Billboard Hot 100. Mitchell’s contributions have also been recognised through numerous honours, including 11 Grammy Awards. Her influence can be heard across generations of musicians who have drawn inspiration from her lyrical precision, melodic experimentation and refusal to remain within conventional boundaries.Mitchell’s relationship with American politics has occasionally entered the public conversation. During a 2024 performance at the Hollywood Bowl, she criticised then-presidential candidate Donald Trump and highlighted the limitations of her status as a Canadian citizen when it came to participating in US elections. Her new citizenship marks a change in that position, giving her the opportunity to take part in the country’s electoral process as an eligible voter.For an artist whose work has become deeply embedded in American cultural history, the development is a personal milestone as well as a notable moment in her long relationship with the country. More than 60 years after arriving from Canada, Mitchell has formally made the United States her adopted home.
Article Summary: Singer-songwriter Joni Mitchell has officially become a United States citizen. The 82-year-old musician shared news of her naturalisation on October 13, 2026, more than six decades after first arriving in the country. Mitchell announced the development on social media, posting a photograph of herself holding a small American flag.

The US administration is considering a $335,000 research and advertising campaign in South Africa to understand why fewer white Afrikaners are applying for refugee status in the United States than officials had expected.According to The Guardian, citing a US state department proposal drafted in August, that the initiative would involve focus groups, a survey of 1,000 Afrikaners and a six-month digital advertising campaign.The proposal said applications had “trended lower than expected” since Afrikaners were allowed to apply directly online in November 2025.The development comes as the administration of President Donald Trump prioritises Afrikaner resettlement while sharply restricting refugee admissions for other groups.Afrikaners are a predominantly Afrikaans-speaking white South African community descended largely from Dutch, French and German settlers who established communities in southern Africa.Trump has repeatedly alleged that white Afrikaners face racial persecution and “white genocide” in South Africa. In February 2025, he signed an executive order directing US officials to prioritise Afrikaner refugee resettlement, citing alleged race-based discrimination and land policies.His administration has also pointed to affirmative action measures and reports of violence against farmers to justify its approach.A US state department spokesperson told The Guardian that Washington continued to process and admit Afrikaners “who are escaping the threat of government-sponsored race-based discrimination”.The South African government has rejected the genocide allegations, maintaining that its land reform and race-based policies are intended to address inequalities created by apartheid rather than persecute white citizens.The dispute has added to tensions between Washington and Pretoria over trade, foreign policy and South Africa's international relationships.

Observe snakes from a safe distance and allow them to move away undisturbed.

A seasonal road with an unusual purpose

A quiet road in southern Illinois has an unusual distinction: it disappears from the traffic map twice a year, leaving snakes, frogs and turtles to cross without the threat of passing cars. Known as Snake Road, the route runs through the Shawnee National Forest between LaRue Swamp and the LaRue-Pine Hills limestone bluffs. National Geographic's educational account describes how the road crosses a seasonal migration route used by snakes and other reptiles moving between the two habitats. Seasonal closures began in 1972, where the road is not permanently closed.The spectacle attracts wildlife enthusiasts hoping to spot dozens of snakes in their natural surroundings, while highlighting how a simple road can become a serious obstacle for migrating wildlife.The animals are not crossing simply because the road happens to be in their way. Their seasonal movements take them between the swamp and the rocky hills on opposite sides.During warmer months, the swamp provides feeding and living areas. When the seasons change, many reptiles head towards the limestone bluffs, where cracks, caves and rocky spaces offer places to shelter during colder weather. The return journey happens in spring.LaRue Road sits directly across this route. That creates a problem because reptiles are often drawn to the road surface when temperatures are cooler in the morning and evening. The warmed pavement can become an attractive place to rest, leaving slow-moving animals exposed to passing vehicles.The area is also home to species that are unusual this far north, including cottonmouths and southern leopard frogs.The decision to restrict traffic dates back to 1972. The road was closed during the migration periods to reduce the number of reptiles being killed by vehicles. The closures were initially unpopular with some people living nearby, according to wildlife officials quoted in reports about Snake Road. Over the years, that opposition eased as the purpose of the restriction became better understood.Today, the road is closed during the spring and autumn migrations. The exact dates cover roughly two months in each season, giving animals a vehicle-free route between the two habitats.For wildlife officials, the arrangement is fairly simple. If cars are removed from a road that thousands of reptiles need to cross, the immediate danger of being struck is removed too.Despite its name, snakes are not the only animals using the route. Frogs, toads and turtles also make the journey between the swamp and the bluffs. As reported by CBS News, there are more than 20 snake species recorded along the road during the autumn period, including three venomous species. Northern copperheads are among them, although they can be difficult to spot in southern Illinois.That does not mean visitors are surrounded by snakes every time they walk the road. Herpetologist Scott Ballard, who has studied the area, has said seeing around 20 snakes during a visit would already be a good day.The road itself is about two and a half miles for a walk there and back. People come not only to look for reptiles but also to walk through the forest and limestone landscape.The geography around Snake Road is an important part of the story. On one side is LaRue Swamp, connected to the wider Mississippi River region. On the other are the LaRue-Pine Hills, where limestone cliffs rise to around 46 metres, as reported.The limestone has weathered into ridges, caves and crevices. These spaces give reptiles places where temperatures are more suitable during the colder months, while the surrounding forest and swamp provide different resources at other times of year. The road happens to run through it. Reptiles are particularly vulnerable on roads because they move slowly and often remain still when approached. A warm road surface can make the danger worse by encouraging them to stop directly in the path of traffic.Snake researcher Rich Seigel has estimated that vehicles have killed close to one in four snakes in the area studied. Across the United States, road deaths have also taken a significant toll on snakes and other reptiles.According to The National Geographic, Wildlife officials, Ballard and Deaton said that they see fewer dead reptiles on the road during the closure.Snakes are often treated as unwanted visitors, but their place in the local food chain is more practical than that reputation suggests. A single snake can consume a substantial amount of prey over the course of a year. Ballard has estimated that one snake can eat around nine pounds of rodents annually. Without predators such as snakes, rodent numbers could rise.Snakes also form part of the diet of other animals, including herons. Removing them from the ecosystem would not simply mean fewer snakes. It would alter the availability of prey and predators around them. That is one reason the migration is treated as a wildlife management issue rather than simply an unusual spectacle.Visitors can walk along Snake Road while vehicles are prohibited during seasonal closures, but encounters with wildlife require caution because some snakes in the area are venomous. Herpetologist Scott Ballard has explained that snakes generally bite when they feel surprised or threatened rather than actively seeking out people. Ballard, who has been bitten several times while working with snakes, said he had never been bitten by a venomous species. His interest in reptiles began at age 10, when he received a pet snake because he was allergic to dogs and cats. That childhood fascination eventually led him to study the snakes around Snake Road.Snake Road remains a functioning route through the Shawnee National Forest, but for several weeks each spring and autumn it serves a different purpose. The traffic signs and barriers give reptiles a rare stretch of road where vehicles are removed from their path.For visitors, the migration offers a chance to see animals moving through a landscape they otherwise might never notice. For the snakes, frogs and turtles, it is simply part of their seasonal movement between the swamp and the limestone hills.The road's unusual status comes from that overlap. It is not closed because the reptiles have taken over the road. It is closed because, for a short period each year, the road cuts directly across a route they have been using for far longer.
Article Summary: Snakes, turtles and frogs share Snake Road’s migration route. The road is closed during the spring and autumn migrations. It gives animals a vehicle-free route between the two habitats. Seasonal closures began in 1972, where the road is not permanently closed.

Article Title: Pakistan ranks lowest in South Asia on hunger index amid rising food prices
Article Text:
Pakistan's 2026 Global Hunger Index standings reveal an alarming crisis, showcasing the worst performance in South Asia amid ongoing economic challenges. (Pic Credit: ANI)

Economic crisis and food inflation worsen Pakistan’s hunger situation

Hunger reduction stalls across South Asia

Extreme weather threatens regional food production

Millions across South Asia continue to face undernourishment

Pakistan has recorded the poorest performance in South Asia in the 2026 global hunger index (GHI), reflecting mounting food insecurity driven by economic instability, rising food prices, climate-related disasters and international conflicts, according to a report by Dawn.Titled “No Security Without Food Security”, the report was jointly prepared by German aid organisation Welthungerhilfe, the institute for international law of peace and armed conflict at Ruhr university Bochum, and swiss organisation helvetas.According to the news agency ANI, the findings indicate that progress in reducing hunger across South Asia has largely stagnated, while Pakistan and Afghanistan have experienced a deterioration in conditions since 2018.Pakistan’s economic challenges and persistent food inflation have eroded household purchasing power, making it increasingly difficult for families to access sufficient and nutritious food.The report noted that Pakistan’s undernourishment indicator had deteriorated from a low level in 2018 to a medium level. Meanwhile, child wasting has approached the threshold associated with the high category, underscoring continuing concerns over child nutrition.South Asia recorded an overall global hunger index score of 23.5, placing the region in the serious category. While the score represents an improvement from 37.5 in 2000, the report suggests that much of the progress was achieved before 2018.Over the past two decades, Pakistan and Afghanistan have moved out of the alarming hunger category. However, persistent levels of child malnutrition continue to pose a significant challenge in both countries.Child stunting has continued to decline in Pakistan, while Afghanistan has recorded a slight increase in the indicator since 2018.Child mortality rates have improved in both countries, falling from very high levels in 2000 to medium levels in the latest assessment.The report also drew attention to the growing impact of extreme weather events on agricultural production and food security across South Asia.Heavy rainfall and flooding damaged crops in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh. In Afghanistan, inadequate rainfall and unusually high temperatures disrupted the cereal-growing season in 2026.These climate-related pressures could further aggravate food shortages and prolong acute food insecurity across the region, according to Dawn.Estimates from the food and agriculture organisation (FAO) indicate that approximately 218 million people across South Asia, including Iran, experienced undernourishment between 2023 and 2025.This represents roughly one-third of the global population affected by undernourishment during the period, highlighting the scale of the region’s food security challenge.The findings underscore the need for sustained efforts to address economic vulnerabilities, improve access to nutritious food and strengthen agricultural resilience against climate-related shocks.
Article Summary: Pakistan has recorded the poorest performance in South Asia in the 2026 global hunger index (GHI) The report was prepared by German aid organisation Welthungerhilfe, the institute for international law of peace and armed conflict at Ruhr university Bochum, and swiss organisation helvetas. The findings indicate that progress in reducing hunger across South Asia has largely stagnated.

Article Title: 33 children, teacher killed as school roof collapses in Pakistan’s Peshawar
Article Text:
18 killed as school roof collapses in Pakistan's Peshawar

At least 33 students and a teacher were killed after the roof of a school collapsed in Pakistan 's Peshawar city on Thursday.Twenty students and a female teacher were killed and more than 40 people injured in the incident, officials said.Peshawar Capital City Police chief Mian Saeed said the incident occurred in Dir Colony in the city's inner area, as cited by PTI.Lady Reading Hospital spokesperson Muhammad Asim said an emergency had been declared at the facility to treat the injured.All the children killed in the incident were aged 13 or younger, Asim said. Rescue officials said 25 injured children had been taken to medical facilities.Rescue teams were clearing the debris and searching for children and school staff who might still be trapped beneath the collapsed structure.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed deep grief over the loss of life and extended his condolences to the bereaved families.Building and roof collapses are common in Pakistan, largely due to poor safety standards and the use of substandard construction materials.In July, three girls aged between three and 13 were killed when part of the outer wall of a government primary school near Umerkot collapsed, burying them under the debris, as cited by Dawn.That same month, a child was killed and at least five others were injured when the roof of an under-construction private school building collapsed in Lahore’s Baghbanpura neighbourhood.In June, 14 children died after the roof of a private tuition centre collapsed in Lahore’s Kahna area. Less than two months earlier, four children were killed and 20 people injured when a classroom roof collapsed at a private school in Dera Ghazi Khan.
Article Summary: Twenty students and a female teacher were killed and more than 40 people injured in the incident. The incident occurred in Dir Colony in the city's inner area. Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed deep grief over the loss of life and extended his condolences to the bereaved families.

Article Title: Pakistan regulator warns TV channels against live coverage of blasts and terror attacks
Article Text:
The regulator also stressed the need for stronger editorial oversight.

Channels told to air only verified information

Legal action for violations

Pakistan's media regulator has warned satellite television channels against broadcasting live footage of explosions, gunfire and terrorist attacks, cautioning that violations could lead to legal action.The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) issued a notification on Tuesday, reminding broadcasters of restrictions first introduced on February 20, 2023. The rules bar news, current affairs and regional-language channels from broadcasting, rebroadcasting or providing live coverage of such incidents.The directive comes as emergency rule has been imposed in the north-western province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, renewing debate over how the media should report security incidents while ensuring that the public receives timely and reliable information.PEMRA has instructed broadcasters to air only “verified information warranted by the relevant government departments or law enforcement agencies”.The regulator also stressed the need for stronger editorial oversight and the effective use of broadcast delays to prevent the immediate transmission of sensitive footage during security incidents.It directed television channels to establish independent editorial boards in line with applicable laws and relevant court judgments.The notification referred to the Supreme Court's judgment in Suo Motu Case No. 28 of 2018 and an Islamabad High Court order dated September 5, 2022, both concerning the prescribed procedure for broadcast delays.PEMRA warned that channels violating the directive could face legal proceedings under Sections 29A, 30 and 33 of the PEMRA Ordinance, 2002, as amended.The latest notification reiterates the regulator's existing restrictions on live coverage of security incidents, with a focus on verification, editorial checks and the use of broadcast delays.
Article Summary: Pakistan's media regulator has warned satellite television channels against broadcasting live footage of explosions, gunfire and terrorist attacks. The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) issued a notification on Tuesday. The rules bar news, current affairs and regional-language channels from broadcasting or providing live coverage of such incidents.

Article Title: 6 killed, several injured as passenger train derails in Pakistan's Punjab
Article Text:
Train travelling from Karachi to Peshawar derails in Pakistan (Representative image) (PTI)

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the top priority to prevent train accidents? Improving railway tracks Upgrading safety systems Regular maintenance and inspections 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion
